claim: Neural injury triggers swift responses from glia, including glial migration and phagocytic clearance of damaged neurons.
source: Neural injury triggers swift responses from glia, including glial migration and phagocytic clearance of damaged neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature and the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1) is induced in Drosophila ensheathing glia responding to severed axons.
source: One factor, matrix metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1), is induced in Drosophila ensheathing glia responding to severed axons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including immunostaining, RNA-seq, and Q-PCR results shown in Figures 4, 5, and 8.

claim: Glial induction of MMP-1 requires the engulfment receptor Draper.
source: Interestingly, glial induction of MMP-1 requires the highly conserved engulfment receptor Draper, as well as AP-1 and STAT92E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that MMP-1 upregulation is blocked in draper mutants (Figure 7a,b) and after Draper RNAi (Figure 8c,d).

claim: Glial induction of MMP-1 requires AP-1.
source: Interestingly, glial induction of MMP-1 requires the highly conserved engulfment receptor Draper, as well as AP-1 and STAT92E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that glial depletion of kayak or Jra (AP-1 subunits) resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction (Figure 7e,f).

claim: Glial induction of MMP-1 requires STAT92E.
source: Interestingly, glial induction of MMP-1 requires the highly conserved engulfment receptor Draper, as well as AP-1 and STAT92E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that glial depletion of STAT92E resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction (Figure 7c,d).

claim: In MMP-1 depleted flies, glia do not properly infiltrate neuropil regions after axotomy.
source: In MMP-1 depleted flies, glia do not properly infiltrate neuropil regions after axotomy and, as a consequence, fail to clear degenerating axonal debris.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced glial membrane expansion in MMP-1 RNAi flies (Figure 9a,c) and altered glial membrane distribution (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).

claim: In MMP-1 depleted flies, glia fail to clear degenerating axonal debris.
source: In MMP-1 depleted flies, glia do not properly infiltrate neuropil regions after axotomy and, as a consequence, fail to clear degenerating axonal debris.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing significantly more OR85e axonal material lingering in the brain of MMP-1 RNAi flies 3 days after injury (Figure 11a,b).

claim: Changes in glial gene expression is one highly conserved feature of glia responding to a range of insults in the CNS.
source: Changes in glial gene expression is one highly conserved feature of glia responding to a range of insults in the CNS (Allen and Barres, 2009; Chung et al., 2013; Doherty et al., 2009; Logan and Freeman, 2007; Logan et al., 2012; Ziegenfuss et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) cascade is one central player in initiating reactive astrocytic and microglial responses to neural damage.
source: Specifically, the janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) cascade is one central player in initiating reactive astrocytic and microglial responses to neural damage (Ben Haim et al., 2015; Herrmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2002; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Glial activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway and the downstream transcriptional heterodimer AP-1 has been reported in various injury and disease models.
source: Glial activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway and the downstream transcriptional heterodimer AP-1, which consists of c-Fos and c-Jun, has also been reported in various injury and disease models (Anderson et al., 1994; Pennypacker et al., 1994; Yu et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Severing adult Drosophila olfactory nerves that project into the antennal lobes of the central brain initiates a classic Wallerian degeneration (WD) program in olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) axons.
source: For example, severing adult Drosophila olfactory nerves that project into the antennal lobes of the central brain initiates a classic Wallerian degeneration (WD) program in olfactory receptor neuron (ORN) axons (Hoopfer et al., 2006; MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Local glia extend membrane projections into the antennal lobe neuropil to phagocytose degenerating axonal and synaptic debris over the course of several days after olfactory nerve injury.
source: Over the course of several days, local glia extend membrane projections into the antennal lobe neuropil to phagocytose degenerating axonal and synaptic debris (Logan and Freeman, 2007; Logan et al., 2012; MacDonald et al., 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The transcription factors AP-1 and STAT92E are acutely induced in Drosophila ensheathing glia in response to axotomy.
source: As in mammals, the transcription factors AP-1 and STAT92E are acutely induced in Drosophila ensheathing glia in response to axotomy (Doherty et al., 2014; Macdonald et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Common molecules are required for glial clearance of engulfment targets across species, including the conserved Draper/MEGF10 receptor, downstream Syk tyrosine kinases, and Rac1-mediated cytoskeletal remodeling.
source: In addition, common molecules are required for glial clearance of engulfment targets across species, including the conserved Draper/MEGF10 receptor, downstream Syk tyrosine kinases, and Rac1-mediated cytoskeletal remodeling (Awasaki et al., 2006; Doherty et al., 2009; Logan and Freeman, 2007; Logan et al., 2012; MacDonald et al., 2006; Scheib et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Axotomy triggers activation of the Draper receptor on local ensheathing glia, which stimulates a positive auto-regulatory transcriptional loop.
source: In adult flies, axotomy triggers activation of the Draper receptor on local ensheathing glia, which, in turn, stimulates a positive auto-regulatory transcriptional loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Doherty et al., 2014) and is consistent with the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: STAT92E becomes activated and targets the draper locus to upregulate draper-I transcript levels after axotomy.
source: Specifically, STAT92E becomes activated and targets the draper locus to upregulate draper-I transcript levels (Doherty et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Draper was robustly upregulated in VNC ensheathing glia after axotomy.
source: Draper is robustly upregulated in VNC ensheathing glia after axotomy
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing Draper upregulation in various injury paradigms (Figure 1c) and by Q-PCR showing draper-I upregulation (Figure 3c).

claim: Removal of a single wing resulted in strong Draper immunofluorescence in the neuropil that contained degenerating projections 24 hr after injury.
source: For example, removal of a single wing or bilateral ablation of the front legs, resulted in strong Draper immunofluorescence in the neuropil that contained degenerating projections corresponding to each injured structure(s) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Bilateral ablation of the front legs resulted in strong Draper immunofluorescence in the neuropil that contained degenerating projections 24 hr after injury.
source: For example, removal of a single wing or bilateral ablation of the front legs, resulted in strong Draper immunofluorescence in the neuropil that contained degenerating projections corresponding to each injured structure(s) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Decapitation elicited robust Draper upregulation throughout the VNC.
source: Similarly, decapitation elicited robust Draper upregulation throughout the VNC (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The adult Drosophila brain contains discrete glial subtypes that vary in location, gene expression, and function.
source: The adult Drosophila brain contains discrete glial subtypes that vary in location, gene expression, and function (Awasaki et al., 2008; Edwards et al., 2012; Freeman, 2015; Hartenstein, 2011; Omoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Cortex glia enwrap neuronal cell bodies throughout the cortex.
source: Cortex glia enwrap neuronal cell bodies throughout the cortex, while neuropil regions contain two unique types of glia: ensheathing glia and astrocytes (Doherty et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Neuropil regions contain two unique types of glia: ensheathing glia and astrocytes.
source: Cortex glia enwrap neuronal cell bodies throughout the cortex, while neuropil regions contain two unique types of glia: ensheathing glia and astrocytes (Doherty et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In the adult olfactory system, ensheathing glia, but not astrocytes, respond to degenerating ORN axons by upregulating draper, invading the neuropil, and clearing axonal debris.
source: In the adult olfactory system, ensheathing glia, but not astrocytes, respond to degenerating ORN axons by upregulating draper, invading the neuropil, and clearing axonal debris (Doherty et al., 2009; Logan and Freeman, 2007; Logan et al., 2012; MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The adult VNC contains similar classes of glia that can be discretely labeled and manipulated with glial subtype-specific genetic drivers.
source: Thus, the adult VNC contains similar classes of glia that can be discretely labeled and manipulated with glial subtype-specific genetic drivers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that different Gal4 drivers label distinct glial populations in the VNC (Figure 2a).

claim: Removal of a single wing resulted in an expansion of ensheathing glial membrane and striking upregulation of Draper around the AMN neuropil on the injured side.
source: Removal of a single wing resulted in an expansion of ensheathing glial membrane and striking upregulation of Draper around the AMN neuropil on the injured side (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Ensheathing glial expression of DraperRNAi largely eliminated the ensheathing glial membrane expansion and Draper increase following left wing injury.
source: Ensheathing glial expression of DraperRNAi largely eliminated the ensheathing glial membrane expansion and Draper increase following left wing injury (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Expression of DraperRNAi in astrocytes did not attenuate injury-induced Draper upregulation following injury to the left wing.
source: In addition, expression of DraperRNAi in astrocytes did not attenuate injury-induced Draper upregulation following injury to the left wing (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: VNC ensheathing glia, but not astrocytes, respond to degenerating axons in the VNC by upregulating Draper.
source: Our results suggest that, as in the olfactory system of the central brain, VNC ensheathing glia, but not astrocytes, respond to degenerating axons in the VNC by upregulating Draper.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Draper upregulation overlaps with ensheathing glial membranes but not astrocyte membranes (Figure 2b,d,e).

claim: Draper is essential for engulfment of degenerating ORN axons in the adult olfactory system.
source: Draper is essential for engulfment of degenerating ORN axons in the adult olfactory system (Doherty et al., 2009; Logan and Freeman, 2007; Logan et al., 2012; MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: No Gr22c GFP+ axonal material was visible in the right (injured) neuropil region 48 hr after transecting the right front leg, while the contralateral Gr22c projection was intact.
source: We transected the right front leg adjacent to the thorax, and imaged Gr22c axons in dissected VNCs after 48 hr. At this time point, no Gr22c GFP+ axonal material was visible in the right (injured) neuropil region, while the contralateral Gr22c projection was intact (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Fragmentation of the severed Gr22c axons was blocked by co-expression of Wlds.
source: Fragmentation of the severed Gr22c axons was blocked by co-expression of Wlds (UAS-Wlds) (Figure 3a), indicating that these axons undergo a classic Wallerian degeneration program post-injury.
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Gr22c axons undergo a classic Wallerian degeneration program post-injury.
source: Fragmentation of the severed Gr22c axons was blocked by co-expression of Wlds (UAS-Wlds) (Figure 3a), indicating that these axons undergo a classic Wallerian degeneration program post-injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Wlds blocks axon fragmentation, which is a hallmark of Wallerian degeneration.

claim: Degenerating Gr22c axons were still detectable in draper mutant flies 48 hr after injury.
source: Notably, degenerating Gr22c axons were still detectable in draper mutant flies (Figure 3a), indicating that Draper is required in multiple regions of the CNS for efficient clearance of axonal debris in adult animals.
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Draper is required in multiple regions of the CNS for efficient clearance of axonal debris in adult animals.
source: Notably, degenerating Gr22c axons were still detectable in draper mutant flies (Figure 3a), indicating that Draper is required in multiple regions of the CNS for efficient clearance of axonal debris in adult animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that degenerating axons persist in draper mutants.

claim: ORN axotomy stimulates activity of the Jra/kayak heterodimer, which is homologous to the AP-1 complex.
source: In the olfactory system, ORN axotomy stimulates activity of two highly conserved transcription factors: (1) the Jra/kayak heterodimer, which is homologous to the AP-1 complex (Macdonald et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ORN axotomy stimulates activity of STAT92E.
source: In the olfactory system, ORN axotomy stimulates activity of two highly conserved transcription factors: (1) the Jra/kayak heterodimer, which is homologous to the AP-1 complex (Macdonald et al., 2013) and (2) STAT92E (Doherty et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: After bilateral ablation of the front legs and wings, robust upregulation of eGFP was observed specifically in the PN and AMN neuropil and surrounding cortical regions using the TRE-eGFP reporter.
source: In uninjured VNC, we observed almost no eGFP signal (not shown), but after bilateral ablation of the front legs and wings, we saw robust upregulation of eGFP specifically in the PN and AMN neuropil and surrounding cortical regions (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Following ablation of front legs and wings, a striking increase in dGFP expression was observed only in the corresponding neuropil regions and surrounding cortex using the 10XSTAT92E-dGFP reporter.
source: dGFP was undetectable in uninjured VNCs (not shown), but following ablation of front legs and wings, we observed a striking increase in dGFP expression only in the corresponding neuropil regions and surrounding cortex (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: AP-1 and STAT92E are activated in VNC glia after axotomy.
source: Together, these results indicate that AP-1 and STAT92E are activated in VNC glia after axotomy and also suggest that common transcriptional programs are stimulated throughout the adult nervous system in response to nerve injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter activation data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Common transcriptional programs are stimulated throughout the adult nervous system in response to nerve injury.
source: Together, these results indicate that AP-1 and STAT92E are activated in VNC glia after axotomy and also suggest that common transcriptional programs are stimulated throughout the adult nervous system in response to nerve injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that similar transcriptional responses occur in both the VNC and olfactory system.

claim: The dee7 promoter fragment contains several requisite STAT92E binding sites for injury-induced activation.
source: Expression is quiescent in the uninjured adult brain, but activated in olfactory ensheathing glia after ORN axotomy, and this promoter fragment contains several requisite STAT92E binding sites for injury-induced activation (Doherty et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: One day after bilateral ablation of front legs and wings, robust activation of dee7-Gal4 was observed throughout the anterior VNC.
source: One day after bilateral ablation of front legs and wings, we consistently observed robust activation throughout the anterior VNC (Figure 3b), which suggests that similar promoter elements in the draper locus are targeted in VNC glia in response to nerve injury.
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Similar promoter elements in the draper locus are targeted in VNC glia in response to nerve injury.
source: One day after bilateral ablation of front legs and wings, we consistently observed robust activation throughout the anterior VNC (Figure 3b), which suggests that similar promoter elements in the draper locus are targeted in VNC glia in response to nerve injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the dee7-Gal4 reporter is activated in the VNC after injury.

claim: draper-I was significantly upregulated in the VNC at all time points (0, 1.5, and 5 hr) in both injury paradigms.
source: draper-I was significantly upregulated in the VNC at all time points in both injury paradigms, with the highest upregulation (~4 fold change) observed 5 hr after all limbs and the head were removed (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is directly supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The highest upregulation of draper-I (~4 fold change) was observed 5 hr after all limbs and the head were removed.
source: draper-I was significantly upregulated in the VNC at all time points in both injury paradigms, with the highest upregulation (~4 fold change) observed 5 hr after all limbs and the head were removed (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is directly supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Peripheral nerve injury induces transcriptional upregulation of draper in the adult VNC.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that peripheral nerve injury induces transcriptional upregulation of draper in the adult VNC and further support the notion that common transcriptional programs are activated in ensheathing glia throughout the adult nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by Q-PCR data (Figure 3c) and reporter activation data (Figure 3b).

claim: An average of 85.2% of the RNA-seq reads mapped to the Drosophila genome.
source: 85.2 ± 0.39% of the reads mapped to the Drosophila genome, with 41.2 ± 2.6% mapping to exons (Purice et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-seq data quality metrics.

claim: 41.2% of the RNA-seq reads mapped to exons.
source: 85.2 ± 0.39% of the reads mapped to the Drosophila genome, with 41.2 ± 2.6% mapping to exons (Purice et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-seq data quality metrics.

claim: Using a cutoff of ≥2 fold DE (adj. p-value<0.01), 306 genes (167 upregulated, 139 downregulated) were identified as differentially expressed.
source: Using a cutoff of ≥2 fold DE (adj. p-value<0.01, Benjamini-Hochberg procedure), we identified 306 genes (167 upregulated, 139 downregulated) (Figure 4b and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the RNA-seq analysis results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Components of the JNK/AP-1 signaling pathway downstream of Draper were upregulated in the RNA-seq screen.
source: Interestingly, components of known innate immunity signaling pathways were included in our list of differentially expressed genes. For example, we detected upregulation of JNK/AP-1 signaling components downstream of Draper, which is consistent with published work describing the role of the JNK/AP-1 pathway during glial recruitment/phagocytic responses to axonal injury in the adult Drosophila olfactory system (Lu et al., 2017; Macdonald et al., 2013) (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4c,d and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Several members of the Spatzle/Toll pathway were upregulated in the RNA-seq screen.
source: In addition, several members of the Spatzle/Toll pathway were upregulated (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is directly supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Nine of ~30 Drosophila genes previously implicated in glial responses to nerve injury (27%) were transcriptionally altered in the RNAseq screen.
source: Finally, to date, only ~30 Drosophila genes have been implicated in glial responses to nerve injury. When mutated, knocked down, or overexpressed in glia, these factors prevent proper clearance of degenerating axons. Nine of these genes (27%) were transcriptionally altered in our RNAseq screen (Figure 4—source data 4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: With the exception of CG6277, all genes tested by Q-PCR were significantly changed in a manner consistent with the RNA-seq data.
source: With the exception of CG6277, all genes were significantly changed in a manner consistent with our RNA-seq data.
evidence: This is directly supported by the Q-PCR validation data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Correlation analysis comparing fold-change for all 10 genes (RNA-seq versus Q-PCR) revealed a Pearson's coefficient of r = 0.860 (p=0.003).
source: Correlation analysis comparing fold-change for all 10 genes (RNA-seq versus Q-PCR) revealed a Pearson's coefficient of r = 0.860 (p=0.003) (Figure 4—source data 5), indicating the robustness of the RNAseq screen to accurately measure the magnitude of differential gene expression.
evidence: This is directly supported by the statistical analysis of the validation data.

claim: MMP-1 was robustly upregulated in injured VNC tissue by RNA-seq analysis (~12 fold).
source: One interesting gene that emerged from this analysis was matrix metalloproteinase-1 (Mmp-1, see Table 1a), which was a top ten Annokey match to our select search terms across all three species (Drosophila, mouse, and human) (Table 1b) and was also robustly upregulated in injured VNC tissue by RNA-seq analysis (~12 fold) (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the RNA-seq data.

claim: MMPs are proteases implicated in extracellular matrix remodeling, cell migration, and metastasis of cancer cells.
source: MMPs are proteases implicated in extracellular matrix remodeling, cell migration, and metastasis of cancer cells (Nagase and Woessner, 1999; Rosenberg, 2002; Verma and Hansch, 2007; Vu and Werb, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: There are over 23 partially redundant MMP genes in mammals.
source: A detailed analysis of MMP function has been hindered by the fact that there are over 23 partially redundant MMP genes in mammals (Page-McCaw et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The Drosophila genome contains only two MMP genes: Mmp-1, a secreted protease, and Mmp-2, which is GPI anchored.
source: In contrast, the Drosophila genome contains only two MMP genes: Mmp-1, a secreted protease, and Mmp-2, which is GPI anchored (Page-McCaw et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A robust increase in MMP-1 was observed in the AMN (wing-innervated) neuropil region on the injured side one day after unilateral wing ablation.
source: We observed a robust increase in MMP-1 in the AMN (wing-innervated) neuropil region on the injured side, and a subset of MMP-1 signal clearly overlapped with ensheathing glial membranes (Figure 5a, white arrows).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A subset of MMP-1 signal clearly overlapped with ensheathing glial membranes after wing injury.
source: We observed a robust increase in MMP-1 in the AMN (wing-innervated) neuropil region on the injured side, and a subset of MMP-1 signal clearly overlapped with ensheathing glial membranes (Figure 5a, white arrows).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: MMP-1 was significantly increased on Western blots of dissected VNC tissue following bilateral ablation of legs and wings.
source: MMP-1 was also significantly increased on Western blots of dissected VNC tissue following bilateral ablation of legs and wings (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5b,c.

claim: All three queried genes (Hairy, MMP-1, and Ets21C) were significantly upregulated in the VNC after injury.
source: All three queried genes were significantly upregulated in the VNC after injury (Hairy, MMP-1, and Ets21C) and, importantly, also in the central brain 3 hr after severing the antennal and maxillary nerves (Figure 5e), further suggesting that common transcriptional cascades are stimulated in central brain and VNC glia after neural injury.
evidence: This is directly supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: All three queried genes (Hairy, MMP-1, and Ets21C) were significantly upregulated in the central brain 3 hr after severing the antennal and maxillary nerves.
source: All three queried genes were significantly upregulated in the VNC after injury (Hairy, MMP-1, and Ets21C) and, importantly, also in the central brain 3 hr after severing the antennal and maxillary nerves (Figure 5e), further suggesting that common transcriptional cascades are stimulated in central brain and VNC glia after neural injury.
evidence: This is directly supported by Q-PCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Common transcriptional cascades are stimulated in central brain and VNC glia after neural injury.
source: All three queried genes were significantly upregulated in the VNC after injury (Hairy, MMP-1, and Ets21C) and, importantly, also in the central brain 3 hr after severing the antennal and maxillary nerves (Figure 5e), further suggesting that common transcriptional cascades are stimulated in central brain and VNC glia after neural injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the same genes are upregulated in both the VNC and central brain after injury.

claim: MMP-1 levels were dramatically increased in the antennal lobe neuropil regions 24 hr after severing both antennal nerves.
source: MMP-1 levels were dramatically increased in the antennal lobe neuropil regions 24 hr after severing both antennal nerves (Figure 5f, middle panel)
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: A striking increase in MMP-1 was observed specifically on maxillary palp glomeruli after bilateral maxillary nerve injury.
source: we also observed a striking increase specifically on maxillary palp glomeruli after bilateral maxillary nerve injury (arrowheads, right panel Figure 5f).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: MMP-1 is acutely upregulated in the adult olfactory system after axotomy.
source: Together, these findings indicate that MMP-1 is acutely upregulated in the adult olfactory system after axotomy.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing MMP-1 upregulation after olfactory nerve injury (Figure 5f).

claim: After antennal nerve injury, overlap of MMP-1 and expanding ensheathing glial membranes was observed but not with astrocytic membranes.
source: Notably, after antennal nerve injury, we observed overlap of MMP-1 and expanding ensheathing glial membranes but not astrocytic membranes (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: MMP-1 accumulation was not observed on uninjured maxillary palp projections despite being surrounded by degenerating antennal ORN axons after antennal nerve injury.
source: Moreover, we do not observe MMP-1 accumulation on uninjured maxillary palp projections (dotted outlined regions in Figure 6c,d) despite the fact they were surrounded by degenerating antennal ORN axons after antennal nerve injury (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: The local increase of MMP-1 in the VNC typically observed after leg injury was undetectable in draper null mutants.
source: Indeed, we found that the local increase of MMP-1 in the VNC typically observed after leg injury (white arrowheads, Figure 7a) was undetectable in draper null mutants (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: In the olfactory system, MMP-1 upregulation was completely blocked in draper−/− flies.
source: Similarly, in the olfactory system, MMP-1 upregulation was completely blocked in draper−/− flies (Figure 7b), indicating that Draper is essential for glial production of MMP-1 in a variety of contexts post-injury.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Draper is essential for glial production of MMP-1 in a variety of contexts post-injury.
source: Similarly, in the olfactory system, MMP-1 upregulation was completely blocked in draper−/− flies (Figure 7b), indicating that Draper is essential for glial production of MMP-1 in a variety of contexts post-injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MMP-1 upregulation is blocked in draper mutants in both the VNC and olfactory system.

claim: Adult specific knockdown of STAT92E in glial cells leads to attenuated MMP-1 response to maxillary palp injury.
source: Adult specific knockdown of STAT92E in glial cells leads to attenuated MMP-1 response to maxillary palp injury. Maximum intensity projections (25 μm) of MMP-1 immunostainings in control and STAT92ERNAi flies.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7c,d.

claim: Glial depletion of STAT92E resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction 24 hr after maxillary nerve axotomy.
source: Interestingly, we found that glial depletion of STAT92E, kayak, or Jra resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction 24 hr after maxillary nerve axotomy (Figure 7c–f).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7c,d.

claim: Adult specific knock down of kay and Jra in glial cells leads to attenuated MMP-1 response to maxillary palp injury.
source: Adult specific knock down of kay and Jra in glial cells leads to attenuated MMP-1 response to maxillary palp injury. Maximum intensity projections (25 μm) of MMP-1 immunostainings in control and RNAi-expressing flies.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Glial depletion of kayak resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction 24 hr after maxillary nerve axotomy.
source: Interestingly, we found that glial depletion of STAT92E, kayak, or Jra resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction 24 hr after maxillary nerve axotomy (Figure 7c–f).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Glial depletion of Jra resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction 24 hr after maxillary nerve axotomy.
source: Interestingly, we found that glial depletion of STAT92E, kayak, or Jra resulted in significant inhibition of MMP-1 induction 24 hr after maxillary nerve axotomy (Figure 7c–f).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Axon injury stimulates the Draper receptor to activate Mmp-1 gene expression in glia, in a STAT92E/AP-1 dependent manner.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that axon injury stimulates the Draper receptor to activate Mmp-1 gene expression in glia, in a STAT92E/AP-1 dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Draper, STAT92E, and AP-1 are all required for MMP-1 upregulation after injury.

claim: Mmp-1 represents the first injury-responsive gene downstream of the Draper/MEGF10 receptor, aside from the positive transcriptional feedback loop described for draper.
source: Aside from the positive transcriptional feedback loop that has been described for draper (Doherty et al., 2014), Mmp-1 now represents the first injury-responsive gene downstream of the Draper/MEGF10 receptor, suggesting that a broader Draper/STAT92E/AP-1 transcriptional program is activated in adult glia following axon injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and comparison to published literature.

claim: A broader Draper/STAT92E/AP-1 transcriptional program is activated in adult glia following axon injury.
source: Aside from the positive transcriptional feedback loop that has been described for draper (Doherty et al., 2014), Mmp-1 now represents the first injury-responsive gene downstream of the Draper/MEGF10 receptor, suggesting that a broader Draper/STAT92E/AP-1 transcriptional program is activated in adult glia following axon injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of MMP-1 as a Draper/STAT92E/AP-1 target gene.

claim: In Mmp-1-LacZ flies, β-gal was almost undetectable in uninjured brains, but levels were dramatically upregulated around the antennal lobes 24 hr after ORN axotomy.
source: We found that in Mmp-1-LacZ flies, β-gal was almost undetectable in uninjured brains, but levels were dramatically upregulated around the antennal lobes 24 hr after ORN axotomy (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8a,b.

claim: A striking overlap was detected between increased ensheathing glial GFP expression in the 10XSTAT92E-dGFP and TRE-GFP flies and β-gal after injury.
source: Notably, we detected a striking overlap between increased ensheathing glial GFP expression in the 10XSTAT92E-dGFP and TRE-GFP flies and β-gal after injury (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8a,b.

claim: MMP-1 production was completely blocked one day after antennal nerve injury after depleting ensheathing glia of Draper.
source: Strikingly, MMP-1 production was completely blocked one day after antennal nerve injury after depleting ensheathing glia of Draper (Figure 8c,d), strongly suggesting that MMP-1 is induced in ensheathing glia following ORN injury, in a Draper-dependent manner.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8c,d.

claim: MMP-1 is induced in ensheathing glia following ORN injury, in a Draper-dependent manner.
source: Strikingly, MMP-1 production was completely blocked one day after antennal nerve injury after depleting ensheathing glia of Draper (Figure 8c,d), strongly suggesting that MMP-1 is induced in ensheathing glia following ORN injury, in a Draper-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ensheathing glial-specific Draper knockdown blocks MMP-1 production.

claim: MMPs can proteolytically target extracellular matrix molecules and influence cell migration, membrane outgrowth and invasion.
source: MMPs can proteolytically target extracellular matrix molecules and influence cell migration, membrane outgrowth and invasion (Brown and Murray, 2015; Nabeshima et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In injured control flies, robust MMP-1 increase was observed, particularly at the periphery of the antennal lobes, in areas overlapping with glial cell bodies and notable glial membrane expansion one day after antennal nerve injury.
source: In injured control flies, we observed a robust MMP-1 increase, particularly at the periphery of the antennal lobes, in areas overlapping with glial cell bodies and notable glial membrane expansion at this timepoint (Figure 9a,b, 'AL Border').
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: Three days after antennal nerve injury, more MMP-1 immunostaining was localized to the central regions of the antennal lobes ('Inside AL'), as compared to the periphery of the antennal lobes ('AL Border').
source: Indeed, three days after antennal nerve injury, we observed more MMP-1 immunostaining localized to the central regions of the antennal lobes ('Inside AL'), as compared to the periphery of the antennal lobes ('AL Border') (Figure 9a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: Glial membrane expansion was significantly reduced in MMP-1RNAi flies one day after antennal nerve axotomy.
source: Importantly, we also found that glial membrane expansion was significantly reduced in MMP-1RNAi flies one day after antennal nerve axotomy (Figure 9a,c)
evidence: This is directly supported by quantification of glial membrane expansion shown in Figure 9a,c.

claim: In control flies, the glial membrane pattern shifts from distinct wrapping of glomeruli to a more diffuse distribution three days after nerve injury.
source: In control flies, the glial membrane pattern shifts from distinct wrapping of glomeruli to a more diffuse distribution three days after nerve injury. This shift in pattern is notably less pronounced in glial MMP-1-depleted flies (Figure 9a,c and Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9a and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: The shift in glial membrane pattern from distinct wrapping of glomeruli to a more diffuse distribution is notably less pronounced in glial MMP-1-depleted flies.
source: In control flies, the glial membrane pattern shifts from distinct wrapping of glomeruli to a more diffuse distribution three days after nerve injury. This shift in pattern is notably less pronounced in glial MMP-1-depleted flies (Figure 9a,c and Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9a and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Antennal nerve injury induces striking cytoskeletal remodeling, which requires activity of the protein phosphatase 4 (PP4) complex and likely also the Rho GTPase Rac1 in responding glia.
source: We have also previously shown that antennal nerve injury induces striking cytoskeletal remodeling, which requires activity of the protein phosphatase 4 (PP4) complex and likely also the Rho GTPase Rac1 in responding glia (Winfree et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In control brains, at both one and three days after antennal injury, increased phalloidin levels mirrored that of expanding glial membranes and MMP-1 expression after injury.
source: In control brains, we found that at both one and three days after antennal injury, increased phalloidin levels mirrored that of expanding glial membranes and MMP-1 expression after injury (Figure 10a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 10a,b.

claim: One day after antennal nerve axotomy, phalloidin staining was most robust at the periphery of the antennal lobes, while staining became more notable internally in the neuropil of the antennal lobe after three days.
source: One day after antennal nerve axotomy, phalloidin staining was most robust at the periphery of the antennal lobes, while staining became more notable internally in the neuropil of the antennal lobe after three days (Figure 10a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 10a,b.

claim: Ensheathing glial expression of MMP-1RNAi strongly attenuated the increase in phalloidin staining at both one and three days after antennal nerve injury.
source: Interestingly, ensheathing glial expression of MMP-1RNAi strongly attenuated the increase in phalloidin staining at both time points (Figure 10a–c).
evidence: This is directly supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 10a-c.

claim: Ensheathing glial generated MMP-1 is essential for proper dynamic glial responses to axotomy in the adult fly brain.
source: Nonetheless, our collective results indicate that ensheathing glial generated MMP-1 is essential for proper dynamic glial responses to axotomy in the adult fly brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that MMP-1 depletion impairs glial membrane expansion and cytoskeletal remodeling.

claim: Significantly more OR85e axonal material lingered in the brain of MMP-1RNAi flies 3 days after injury.
source: Significantly more OR85e axonal material lingered in the brain of MMP-1RNAi flies 3 days after injury (arrowheads Figure 11a,b).
evidence: This is directly supported by quantification of axonal debris shown in Figure 11a,b.

claim: MMP-1 accumulation on severed nerves was significantly reduced in MMP-1-depleted animals.
source: We also confirmed that MMP-1 accumulation on severed nerves was significantly reduced in MMP-1-depleted animals (arrows Figure 11a,c).
evidence: This is directly supported by quantification of MMP-1 fluorescence shown in Figure 11a,c.

claim: TIMP overexpression delayed clearance of degenerating axons 3 days after injury.
source: We expressed UAS-TIMP in adult glial cells, quantified OR85e GFP+ axons 3 days after nerve injury, and importantly, found that TIMP overexpression also delayed clearance of degenerating axons 3 days after injury (Figure 11d,e).
evidence: This is directly supported by quantification of axonal debris shown in Figure 11d,e.

claim: Draper-dependent activation of MMP-1 is essential for ensheathing glia to invade neuropil regions and properly clear degenerating axonal debris after nerve injury.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that Draper-dependent activation of MMP-1 is essential for ensheathing glia to invade neuropil regions and properly clear degenerating axonal debris after nerve injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that MMP-1 is required for glial infiltration and axonal debris clearance.

claim: The fundamental components of innate glial immune responses to neurodegeneration are strikingly similar in flies and vertebrates.
source: The fundamental components of innate glial immune responses to neurodegeneration are strikingly similar in flies and vertebrates.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the broader scientific literature and the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: In mammals, acute insults such as spinal cord injury and stroke, activate numerous transcriptional cascades in reactive glia.
source: In mammals, acute insults such as spinal cord injury and stroke, activate numerous transcriptional cascades in reactive glia (Herrmann et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2002; Park et al., 2016; Pennypacker et al., 1994; Yu et al., 1995), but ascribing specific physiological roles to each member of the pathway is an ongoing and challenging endeavor.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The adult VNC injury assay revealed cohorts of upregulated genes implicated in innate immunity in other phagocytic Drosophila cell types and in both professional and amateur vertebrate phagocytes.
source: Our assay revealed cohorts of upregulated genes implicated in innate immunity in other phagocytic Drosophila cell types and in both professional and amateur vertebrate phagocytes, including members of the Toll-like signaling pathway, which validates the adult VNC injury assay as a reliable model to explore prospective cascades that govern innate glial responses.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data showing upregulation of known innate immunity genes (Figure 4c,d).

claim: The VNC harvests likely contain some transcripts upregulated in neurons projecting to peripheral injured structures because a glial-specific isolation strategy was not utilized.
source: We should note that because our VNC harvests did not utilize a glial-specific isolation strategy, our dataset likely contains some transcripts upregulated in neurons projecting to peripheral injured structures.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the experimental design.

claim: Mammalian CNS motor neuron axons do not regenerate after mechanical or ischemic injury unless intrinsic proregenerative transcriptional programs are activated through neuron preconditioning.
source: Notably, mammalian CNS motor neuron axons do not regenerate after mechanical or ischemic injury unless intrinsic proregenerative transcriptional programs are activated through neuron preconditioning (Neumann and Woolf, 1999; Neumann et al., 2002; Qiu et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Similar axonal regeneration programs have been defined in Drosophila larval motoneurons, including retrograde pathways that require the highly conserved mediators dual leucine zipper kinase (DLK) and cAMP/PKA.
source: Similar axonal regeneration programs have been defined in Drosophila larval motoneurons, including retrograde pathways that require the highly conserved mediators dual leucine zipper kinase (DLK) and cAMP/PKA (Brace and DiAntonio, 2017; Hao et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Some groups have shown that adult Drosophila neurons do have some capacity, albeit limited, to regenerate after an injury event.
source: Robust axon regeneration models have not yet been fully developed in adult flies, although some groups have shown that adult Drosophila neurons do have some capacity, albeit limited, to regenerate after an injury event (Ayaz et al., 2008; Soares et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MMP genes are regulated by JNK signaling, AP-1 and/or STAT92E.
source: Our AP-1 and STAT92E loss of function results mirror findings in other organisms that report MMP genes are regulated by JNK signaling, AP-1 and/or STAT92E (Chakraborti et al., 2003; Korzus et al., 1997; Stevens and Page-McCaw, 2012), highlighting the AP-1/STAT92E/MMP-1 cascade as an evolutionarily conserved module of innate glial immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The AP-1/STAT92E/MMP-1 cascade is an evolutionarily conserved module of innate glial immunity.
source: Our AP-1 and STAT92E loss of function results mirror findings in other organisms that report MMP genes are regulated by JNK signaling, AP-1 and/or STAT92E (Chakraborti et al., 2003; Korzus et al., 1997; Stevens and Page-McCaw, 2012), highlighting the AP-1/STAT92E/MMP-1 cascade as an evolutionarily conserved module of innate glial immunity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and comparison to published literature.

claim: Previous work has demonstrated a requisite role for Draper during infiltration of Drosophila neuropil after olfactory nerve injury.
source: Previous work has demonstrated a requisite role for Draper during infiltration of Drosophila neuropil after olfactory nerve injury (MacDonald et al., 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2012), but the molecular mechanisms were unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: This work is the first to couple Draper to a transcriptional cascade that actively promotes extracellular matrix remodeling and glial cell motility via MMP-1 induction.
source: Our work is now the first to couple Draper, which is classically considered an engulfment recognition receptor (Chung et al., 2015; Logan et al., 2012; Tasdemir-Yilmaz and Freeman, 2014; Zhou et al., 2001), to a transcriptional cascade that we propose actively promotes extracellular matrix remodeling and glial cell motility via MMP-1 induction.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the current study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: MMPs can cleave extracellular matrix molecules to accommodate increased cell migration in a variety of organs and cell types, including metastatic cancer cells.
source: Indeed, MMPs can cleave extracellular matrix molecules to accommodate increased cell migration in a variety of organs and cell types, including metastatic cancer cells (Al-Alem and Curry, 2015; Deryugina and Quigley, 2015; Page-McCaw, 2008; Thakur and Bedogni, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: MMPs can target specific ligands or receptors to reveal cryptic sites and modulate intercellular signaling.
source: MMPs can also target specific ligands or receptors to reveal cryptic sites and modulate intercellular signaling (Bauvois, 2012; Chakraborti et al., 2003; Page-McCaw et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In response to adult antennal nerve axotomy, activation of the ensheathing glial receptor Draper is required for the production of the secreted protease MMP-1 in ensheathing glial cells within 24 hr.
source: Here, we show that in response to adult antennal nerve axotomy, activation of the ensheathing glial receptor Draper is required for the production of the secreted protease MMP-1 in ensheathing glial cells within 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Draper is required for MMP-1 upregulation (Figures 7, 8).

claim: Loss of MMP-1 inhibits dynamic membrane expansion of ensheathing glia and delays glial clearance of degenerating olfactory receptor neuron axons.
source: Our results also reveal that loss of MMP-1 inhibits dynamic membrane expansion of ensheathing glia and delays glial clearance of degenerating olfactory receptor neuron axons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced glial membrane expansion (Figure 9) and delayed axonal debris clearance (Figure 11) in MMP-1 depleted flies.

claim: Released MMP-1 remodels the extracellular matrix to facilitate ensheathing glial infiltration into the inner regions of the antennal lobes that house a large number of degenerating axons.
source: We favor a model in which released MMP-1 remodels the extracellular matrix – and perhaps transmembrane molecules (e.g. adhesion factors) - to facilitate ensheathing glial infiltration into the inner regions of the antennal lobes that house a large number of degenerating axons.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and known functions of MMPs.

claim: Secreted MMP-1 may also cleave factors on degenerating axons to encourage fragmentation or release peptide fragments that serve as secondary ligands to further stimulate responses from local ensheathing glia.
source: However, we can't exclude the possibility that secreted MMP-1 also cleaves factors on degenerating axons to encourage fragmentation or perhaps even release peptide fragments that serve as secondary ligands to further stimulate responses from local ensheathing glia.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative model proposed by the authors.

claim: One molecule cleaved by Drosophila MMP-1 during development is the transmembrane adhesion factor NinjurinA (NinjA).
source: One molecule cleaved by Drosophila MMP-1 during development is the transmembrane adhesion factor NinjurinA (NinjA).
evidence: This claim is supported by the broader scientific literature on MMP-1 substrates.

claim: MMP-1 cleavage of NinjA on the surface of tracheal cells is essential for proper branching and formation of a mature tracheal system.
source: Most organs of the fly contain an intricate tracheal network that transports essential gases or fluids (Samakovlis et al., 1996), and MMP-1 cleavage of NinjA on the surface of tracheal cells is essential for proper branching and formation of a mature tracheal system (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ninjurins were initially identified by screening for upregulated genes in a rodent nerve injury assay.
source: Interestingly, Ninjurins are a conserved family of factors that were initially identified by screening for upregulated genes in a rodent nerve injury assay (Araki and Milbrandt, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: One or more Ninjurins are upregulated in injury, stress, and inflammation models.
source: Several groups have since confirmed that one or more Ninjurins are upregulated in injury, stress, and inflammation models, although the specific function of Ninjurins is still unclear (Jennewein et al., 2015; Koike et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: NinjA was upregulated in the VNC injury screen.
source: Intriguingly, NinjA was also upregulated in our VNC injury screen (Figure 4d and Figure 4—source data 2), and it will be interesting to explore a potential mechanistic connection between MMP-1 and NinjA in the context of glial recruitment to injury sites and phagocytic clearance of degenerating axonal debris.
evidence: This is directly supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Drosophila MMP-1 is secreted, while MMP-2 is GPI-anchored.
source: Drosophila MMP-1 is secreted, while MMP-2 is GPI-anchored (Page-McCaw, 2008), and it remains unclear whether MMP-2 also contributes to innate glial immunity in the adult fly brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: MMP-9 levels are significantly increased in the CA1 region of the hippocampus after induction of late-phase long-term potentiation (L-LTP).
source: For example, MMP-9 levels are significantly increased in the CA1 region of the hippocampus after induction of late-phase long-term potentiation (L-LTP) (Huntley, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of MMP-9 blocks not only L-LTP, but also the spine enlargement that is typically associated with persistent LTP.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of MMP-9 blocks not only L-LTP, but also the spine enlargement that is typically associated with persistent LTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by the broader scientific literature on MMP-9 function.

claim: MMP-9 is sufficient to promote synaptic structural remodeling, likely through proteolytic cleavage of integrins and/or integrin ligands.
source: Conversely, gain of function experiments have revealed that MMP-9 is sufficient to promote synaptic structural remodeling, likely through proteolytic cleavage of integrins and/or integrin ligands (Huntley, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: High levels of MMP activity or expression could contribute to maladaptive wiring after acute injury and in disease states.
source: These recent findings introduce new concerns for how pathological release of MMPs might influence neural circuitry and function. High levels of MMP activity or expression could contribute to maladaptive wiring after acute injury and in disease states.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the potential implications of the findings.

claim: The Draper receptor, STAT, AP-1, and MMP family of secreted proteases are all highly conserved.
source: Given that the Draper receptor, STAT, AP-1, and MMP family of secreted proteases are all highly conserved, we anticipate that our work will provide new insight into how MEGF10 mechanistically contributes to glial engulfment of apoptotic neurons and synaptic/axonal clearance, as well as functional neuronal recovery, in mammals.
evidence: This is supported by the broader scientific literature on the conservation of these molecules.
